validated_work_order.understanding:
PR #103 (for #97) split ReportTableList's key guard into two test files so each React warning sentence could be asserted where its warning budget allows, and dropped one assertion in the move. The split is correct about the mechanism it fixed — React emits the missing-key sentence at most once per test FILE, so a guard sharing a file with another render goes vacuously green — but the move took the uuid fixture (two real categories as siblings, the exact shape that collides under a wrong key expression for real rows) into the file asserting only the missing-key sentence and left its duplicate-key assertion behind. I reproduced the consequence myself rather than taking it on trust: on the shipped tree, mutating ReportTableList.tsx:84 to key={String(category.uncategorizedId)} — which keys both real categories to the string 'undefined' — gives Tests 3 passed (3), fully green, where main failed 1 of 4. Three of the five review findings are this one root cause seen from different angles.

Note for anyone reading the tree: ReportTableList.test.tsx holds DUPLICATE_KEY_WARNING and the two collision tests; ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx holds MISSING_KEY_WARNING and the one missing-key test.
validated_work_order.root_cause: The file split is forced by the missing-key sentence's once-per-file budget and is correct. The assertion split that followed it was wrong: it moved the only fixture that renders two real categories into a file that asserts only one of the two sentences that fixture can emit, so the duplicate-key half of the guard stopped existing anywhere. A second, independent cause compounds it: the two files duplicate their scaffolding verbatim, so a fix to one half has to be hand-copied to the other.
validated_work_order.approach:
Three changes, all in test files. No production code changes — ReportTableList.tsx's key expression is correct and stays byte-for-byte as it is.

1. Restore the lost capability (finding 0). In ReportTableList.missingKey.test.tsx, split the console.error read into a shared consoleErrors() and add DUPLICATE_KEY_WARNING = /same key/i beside MISSING_KEY_WARNING, asserting both sentences on that file's single render. Safe because the two sentences have independent budgets: the file renders exactly one fixture, and the duplicate-key sentence is not deduplicated per file.

2. Merge the mixed-sibling fixture in and assert BOTH sentences on it (findings 2 and 3) — this is the step the previous plan got wrong, and the arbiter has verified it behaviourally. Adding uuid-1/Rent to the collision fixture makes that fixture capable of emitting the missing-key sentence too (under key={category.uncategorizedId} the real category is keyless), so asserting only the duplicate-key sentence there would leave a sentence unasserted with nothing standing behind it. Rather than exempting the fixture, the collision test asserts both sentences on its one render. Verified live and sentence-specific: under key={category.uncategorizedId} it fails at the missing-key assertion (line 107), under key={category.id} at the duplicate-key assertion (line 106, 2 warnings captured). Delete the mixed-sibling test outright — it had no detection power the surviving test lacked, and under this design a second render in that file would contest the missing-key budget and void an assertion the design depends on.

3. Extract the duplicated scaffolding (finding 4). Create ReportTableList.fixtures.tsx exporting groupEntity, dataEntity, renderRow and consoleErrors; both test files import from it. The two *.test.tsx files stay separate — that separation is load-bearing. Only the raw console.error read is shared; each file keeps its own sentence patterns, because which sentence a file owns is the thing the split is about.

acceptance.check: Every key expression that is behaviourally DIFFERENT from the shipped one is matched by a test that fails under it. The exact failure sets, all measured by the arbiter against a build of this design: key={category.id} fails ONLY the collision test (1 failed | 1 passed); key={String(category.uncategorizedId)} fails ONLY the missing-key test (1 failed | 1 passed); key={category.uncategorizedId} and key={category.id ?? category.uncategorizedId} each fail BOTH tests (2 failed) — the collision fixture's real category is keyless under the first, so its own missing-key assertion fires too; the shipped key={category.uncategorizedId ?? category.id} passes both.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Run the mutant matrix in qa_script and compare each failure set against the one stated here. key={category.uncategorizedId} failing BOTH tests is correct and expected, not a defect — AC-4 as written requires it, since the collision fixture can emit that sentence. The excluded expressions — key={category.uncategorizedId ?? String(category.id)}, key={category.uncategorizedId ?? category.name.toLowerCase()} and key={category.name} — are NOT required to fail: each produces keys identical to the shipped expression on every row of both fixtures, or collides only names differing in case, so no key-warning assertion could ever see them. GroupedEntity.id is typed string, so String(category.id) is identity on every row.

acceptance.check: groupEntity, dataEntity, renderRow and the console.error read are declared once, in ReportTableList.fixtures.tsx, and neither *.test.tsx file declares its own copy. The two *.test.tsx files still exist separately.

acceptance.check: Each React sentence is matched by a filter that is not subsumed by another, and every fixture capable of producing a given sentence asserts it. This criterion is behavioural, not structural: it does NOT require one sentence per file, and it does NOT exempt any fixture. The structural rule that forbade the missing-key file from containing /same key/i is what caused the regression and is not carried forward. Both of this design's fixtures assert both sentences, so the clause holds as written and nothing needs exempting.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Two checks, because the clause has two halves. (a) Filters are distinct and non-subsuming: MISSING_KEY_WARNING and DUPLICATE_KEY_WARNING are separate constants in each file, and /same key/i does not match the missing-key sentence or vice versa. (b) The capability half is tested BEHAVIOURALLY, by mutating: key={category.uncategorizedId} makes the collision fixture emit the missing-key sentence, and the collision test MUST fail — if it passes, that fixture can produce the sentence with no assertion standing behind it and the criterion is violated. The arbiter ran exactly this: the collision test fails with AssertionError receiving 'Each child in a list should have a unique "key" prop.' at the missingKeyWarnings() assertion, while key={category.id} makes the same test fail at the duplicateKeyWarnings() assertion instead with 2 captured 'Encountered two children with the same key' warnings. Both assertions are live and sentence-specific, which is the property AC-4 exists to enforce.

acceptance.check: No comment in either file claims the mixed real-plus-synthetic fixture is a production shape. The comment states instead that it is deliberately adversarial, and that categoryLists() builds the three synthetic rows as their own top-level group with no real category in it.

risks: ReportTableList.fixtures.tsx is a non-test .tsx module inside src/. It is reachable only from the two test files and no production code imports it, so it cannot enter a bundle, but it does join the desktop-client TypeScript program. Typecheck and lint were run against it and both pass.

The collision file's fixture is deliberately adversarial: it holds a real category where production would hold only synthetic rows. If categoryLists() is ever changed to merge synthetic rows into real groups, that fixture becomes the only thing covering the shape — which is the intent, but it means the file's coverage claim runs ahead of the production shape. Stated in the comment itself, per AC-5.

Both files now assert both sentences, so a future second render in EITHER file would contest the missing-key budget and silently void one assertion. Nothing enforces 'one render per file' mechanically; it rests on the header comment and on each file having exactly one test today. This is a residual risk, not a guarded invariant.
If a future React version rewords either warning, both filters are tail-anchored (/same key/i, /unique .?key.? prop/i) so a reworded prefix is caught, but a reworded tail is not.

alternatives_considered.approach: Route A — keep the merged collision fixture asserting only the duplicate-key sentence, and narrow AC-4 clause 2 so the fixture is exempt (scoping it to the sentence a fixture's own rows can collide on, or noting a keyless row there is caught by the missing-key file's uncontested render). This was the other option the previous review offered.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It requires writing an exemption into AC-4 for a fixture that demonstrably emits the missing-key sentence, so the criterion has to be qualified rather than met, and the next reviewer reads it as the same regression recurring. Route B meets AC-4 clause 2 exactly as originally written, which is why I kept it despite Route A being the smaller diff. The cost is honest and stated in AC-2 and qa_script: key={category.uncategorizedId} fails BOTH tests, because the collision fixture's own missing-key assertion fires. That is a fact about the design, not a defect, and it is written into every downstream expectation rather than left as a stale one for QA to fail a correct implementation over.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the mixed-sibling test and reword its comment to call it a defensive guard over a shape production does not build (the reviewer's second option under finding 3).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Under every mutant I ran it failed and passed as a pair with the test above it, so it has no detection power the first lacks. Keeping it preserves a second render, which now carries a real cost: a second render in the collision file would contest the file's once-per-file missing-key budget and silently void one of the two assertions Route B depends on. Folding uuid-1 into the surviving fixture covers both shapes in one render; the detection is identical.

alternatives_considered.approach: Merge the two test files back into one and rely on ordering to work around the once-per-file missing-key budget.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is exactly the arrangement PR #103 removed and the reason still holds: whichever test renders first consumes the budget and the other goes vacuously green. Under this design that would be worse, not better — with both fixtures asserting both sentences, a single file would spend its missing-key budget once and void an assertion. The split is load-bearing; only the scaffolding around it is not.

alternatives_considered.approach: Replace the per-sentence regexes with a single filter matching any React key warning, so one assertion covers both sentences in each file.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: That restores the subsumption the original array had — a filter matching both sentences can never distinguish which half of the key expression broke, so a duplicate-key regression would report as a missing-key failure. Two tail-anchored patterns, each filtered separately, is the minimum that keeps a failure attributable, and it is what makes AC-4's non-subsumption half checkable.

assumptions: That each file's single render still spends its own file's missing-key budget exactly once after the change. Consistent with my own runs — each file has exactly one test, and key={category.uncategorizedId} produces one failure per file, not two — but React's warning bookkeeping was not instrumented directly; this is inherited from PR #103's measurement.

That the duplicate-key sentence is not deduplicated per file. This is what makes asserting both sentences on one render safe, and what lets the collision file fail on its duplicate-key assertion. Inherited from PR #103, and consistent with my own runs: key={category.id} captured 2 warnings from the collision fixture's single render.
That no test outside this directory imports either test file. I grepped and found none; the vitest include and the Playwright/E2E suites are disjoint from *.test.tsx under src/.

That a desktop-client vitest run scoped to this directory is representative of the full suite. Both files call vi.restoreAllMocks() in afterEach and pass standalone and together; I did not run the full yarn test across all workspaces.
That 'chore' is the right kind: no user-visible behaviour changes, and no production code is touched.

That this issue carries no '## Acceptance (from the split)' section. Verified two ways: the issue body has no such heading and the ledger at origin/sdlc-state:state/104.json has an empty acceptance array. So no criterion needs a source id.

validated_work_order.debate_summary:
There was no critique to judge: plan/critique.json is empty ({}), for the second plan attempt running. The council's second voice produced nothing, so rather than record a tidy consensus I re-verified the proposal's load-bearing claims myself, in the tree, by building its design and running the matrix. That was worth doing because the previous plan for this issue was rejected on a specific self-consistency defect — AC-4's clause 2 was violated by the plan's own files[] prescription — and a claim that needed checking was exactly the kind that slipped through last time.

On the defect that got the last plan rejected: this proposal takes Route B and commits to it, and I confirmed it actually holds rather than taking the word for it. Adding uuid-1/Rent to the collision fixture does make that fixture capable of emitting the missing-key sentence, so asserting only the duplicate-key one would have repeated the same violation. This proposal instead asserts BOTH sentences on that fixture's single render, and I verified both assertions are live and sentence-specific: under key={category.uncategorizedId} the collision test fails at line 107 with the missing-key sentence, and under key={category.id} it fails at line 106 with two captured duplicate-key warnings. Neither is a vacuous pass. The cost the previous review flagged is accepted openly rather than hidden: key={category.uncategorizedId} now fails BOTH tests, and AC-2, the qa_script mutant step and the tests[] case all say so, with an explicit instruction not to fail QA over it. I re-ran that mutant myself and got 2 failed (2), matching what is written down. This is the defect the previous plan would have shipped: a work order telling the implementer to build something its own acceptance criteria forbid.

The proposal also fixes the second half of that review — AC-4's how_to_verify previously tested only that two patterns were distinct, so the clause actually being violated was the one QA was never asked to look at. It now has two checks matching its two halves, and the capability half is behavioural: mutate to key={category.uncategorizedId} and require the collision test to fail. I ran that check.

What I changed against the proposal: two things. AC-6 and the final qa_script step previously said `yarn lint:fix`, which rewrites plan/proposal.json and plan/critique.json — untracked pipeline artifacts that have nothing to do with this change. I scoped the lint check to the source directory so QA is not sent to fix files outside the work order. And I added to files[] an instruction to leave the afterEach block in each test file, which finding 4 lists among the duplicated scaffolding but which should not move into a shared helper: a side-effecting import from a fixtures module is worse than the two-line duplication. That is a deviation from the proposal's silence on the point, in the direction of less consolidation.

On the five findings: all still reproduce against the current tree, and none is stale, which the issue explicitly asked to be checked. Finding 0 is real — I watched the shipped tree pass String(category.uncategorizedId) 3/3, and watch it fail exactly the missing-key test once the fix is in. Findings 2 and 4 I confirmed by reading (ReportOptions.ts:375-381 and :403-406; the byte-identical helpers and the vitest include that keeps a fixtures.tsx out of collection). Finding 3 — the mixed-sibling test being redundant — I accept over the reviewer's objection that it 'has verified discriminating power and should stay', since the reviewer's own evidence undercuts that: the discriminating power it cites applies equally to the test above. The one place this knowingly departs from a reviewer preference is deleting that test, and the justification is now stronger than the last plan's: under Route B a second render in that file would contest the missing-key budget and void an assertion the design depends on, so keeping it is not merely redundant but actively unsafe. Finding 1 is dismissed as un-actionable, agreeing with the proposal — the AC-4 text it objects to lives in a work order for shipped issue #97, not in this repository, so there is nothing to edit, and AC-4 here answers its diagnosis by being behavioural.

One thing a human should weigh: Route A versus Route B is a real choice, not a forced one, and I picked B because it satisfies AC-4 as written rather than qualifying it. The diff between them is about two lines.
residual_risks: key={category.uncategorizedId ?? String(category.id)}, key={category.uncategorizedId ?? category.name.toLowerCase()} and key={category.name} stay green, as they did on main and on the PR. The first is provably equivalent to the shipped expression (GroupedEntity.id is typed string) and no test can ever catch it. The other two collide only categories whose names differ only in case, and no fixture contains such a pair. Catching them would mean adding a case-colliding fixture — beyond this ticket. QA should look here first if name-keyed mutants are the concern.

The once-per-file missing-key budget is now relied upon in BOTH files, and nothing enforces 'exactly one render per file' mechanically. Today each file has exactly one test, so each budget is spent once. A future second render in either file would spend the budget twice and silently void one of the two assertions this design depends on. It rests on the header comments and on the test count, not on an assertion.

The duplicate-key half of the guard is now asserted in both files rather than one, which is the redundancy that makes AC-4 hold without an exemption. If someone later concludes the collision file's duplicate-key assertion is 'obviously also covered' and deletes it, AC-4's capability clause is still satisfied but the file no longer fails on its own sentence — AC-2's exact failure sets in qa_script are what would catch that, so do not treat those numbers as approximate.

The merged fixture is deliberately adversarial: it holds a real category where production holds only synthetic rows. If categoryLists() is ever changed to merge synthetic rows into real groups, this fixture is the only thing covering that shape — the intent, but the file's coverage claim runs ahead of the production shape.
The full desktop-client suite was not run — only vitest scoped to this directory, plus typecheck and lint. An unrelated test that imports these files would not have been caught by what I ran.
